cards.question: When should surgical antibiotic prophylaxis be given?
cards.answer: Within 60 min before knife-to-skin (within 120 min for vancomycin or fluoroquinolones — slow infusions). Re-dose intra-operatively if procedure exceeds 2 × antibiotic half-life or blood loss >1500 mL. Single dose usually sufficient; continuing beyond 24 h does not reduce SSI but selects for resistance. Allergy: cefuroxime is safe in penicillin allergy unless anaphylaxis (cross-reactivity <1 %); use clindamycin or teicoplanin if severe.

cards.question: What are the indications for vancomycin therapeutic drug monitoring?
cards.answer: Narrow therapeutic index; nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Target AUC₂₄ 400–600 mg·h/L (preferred) or trough 15–20 mg/L for serious infections. Monitor pre-4th dose, daily in unstable renal function, every 3–4 days when stable. Loading dose 25–30 mg/kg (actual body weight, max 3 g) gives faster therapeutic levels. Slow infusion ≥1 g/h reduces red-man syndrome (histamine release).

cards.question: What is the difference between concentration-dependent and time-dependent killing?
cards.answer: Concentration-dependent (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole) — efficacy correlates with Cmax/MIC ratio; give large doses at extended intervals (once-daily gentamicin). Time-dependent (β-lactams, vancomycin) — efficacy correlates with time above MIC; give frequent doses or extended/continuous infusion (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam continuous infusion in severe sepsis). Aminoglycoside post-antibiotic effect supports once-daily dosing.
